expectedText:
WHISTLEBLOWER POLICY
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

WHO THIS POLICY'S FEDERAL PROTECTIONS COVER
This policy's protections under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act apply if Acme, Inc. has a class of securities registered under the Securities Exchange Act, is required to file reports under Exchange Act section 15(d), is a subsidiary or affiliate whose financial information is included in such a company's consolidated financial statements, or is a nationally recognized statistical rating organization. They extend to that company's officers, employees, contractors, subcontractors, and agents — not just to the company directly.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "No company with a class of securities registered under section 12 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, covered-company definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1514A)
  "any officer, employee, contractor, subcontractor, or agent of such company or nationally recognized statistical rating organization, may discharge, demote, suspend, threaten, harass, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee in the terms and conditions of employment because of any lawful act done by the employee"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, extension to officers, employees, contractors, and agents (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1514A)
  "We hold, based on the text of § 1514A, the mischief to which Congress was responding, and earlier legislation Congress drew upon, that the provision shelters employees of private contractors and subcontractors, just as it shelters employees of the public company served by the contractors and subcontractors."
  — Lawson v. FMR LLC, 571 U.S. 429 (2014) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2655498/lawson-v-fmr-llc/)
  Known gap: This is federal law written for public companies and their contractor and agent relationships, not a general private-sector whistleblower rule — a privately held company with no ties to a public company isn't covered by this specific statute. Many states have their own whistleblower-protection laws for private employers that this document doesn't state.

WHAT COUNTS AS A PROTECTED REPORT
Protected reports include providing information, or otherwise assisting in an investigation, about conduct an employee reasonably believes violates mail, wire, bank, or securities fraud law, an SEC rule, or federal law prohibiting fraud against shareholders — as long as the report goes to a federal regulatory or law enforcement agency, a Member or committee of Congress, or a supervisor or other person at the company with authority to investigate or address the misconduct. Filing, testifying in, or otherwise assisting a related legal proceeding is protected the same way.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "to provide information, cause information to be provided, or otherwise assist in an investigation regarding any conduct which the employee reasonably believes constitutes a violation of section 1341, 1343, 1344, or 1348, any rule or regulation of the Securities and Exchange Commission, or any provision of Federal law relating to fraud against shareholders"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, protected-activity definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1514A)
  "a person with supervisory authority over the employee (or such other person working for the employer who has the authority to investigate, discover, or terminate misconduct)"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, internal-supervisor reporting channel (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1514A)
  "to file, cause to be filed, testify, participate in, or otherwise assist in a proceeding filed or about to be filed (with any knowledge of the employer) relating to an alleged violation of section 1341, 1343, 1344, or 1348, any rule or regulation of the Securities and Exchange Commission, or any provision of Federal law relating to fraud against shareholders."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, participation in a related proceeding (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1514A)
  Known gap: The standard is a reasonable, good-faith belief — a report doesn't have to turn out to be correct, or ever be proven in court, to be protected. This protects an internal report to a supervisor just as much as a report to an outside regulator; treating only external regulatory complaints as 'real' whistleblowing applies a narrower standard than the statute sets. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (18 U.S.C. § 1514A) rather than independently authored sources; no corroborating case on the reasonable-belief standard was added here.

A SEPARATE, NARROWER PROTECTION FOR SEC REPORTS
A different federal law, the Dodd-Frank Act, adds its own anti-retaliation right — with a direct right to sue in federal court and a longer filing deadline — but only for someone who meets Dodd-Frank's own definition of 'whistleblower': a person who has actually reported information to the Securities and Exchange Commission itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "[t]he term “whistleblower” means any individual who provides, or 2 or more individuals acting jointly who provide, information relating to a violation of the securities laws to the Commission, in a manner established, by rule or regulation, by the Commission"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 78u-6(a)(6) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Dodd-Frank Act, whistleblower definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/78u-6)
  "Dodd-Frank’s anti-retaliation provision does not extend to an individual, like Somers, who has not reported a violation of the securities laws to the SEC."
  — Digital Realty Trust, Inc. v. Somers, 583 U.S. 149 (2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4469602/digital-realty-trust-inc-v-somers/)
  "An individual who alleges discharge or other discrimination in violation of subparagraph (A) may bring an action under this subsection in the appropriate district court of the United States for the relief provided in subparagraph (C)."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 78u-6(h)(1)(B)(i) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Dodd-Frank Act, the direct right to sue in federal court (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/78u-6)
  Known gap: This is a distinct, narrower category from the Sarbanes-Oxley protection above. The Supreme Court held that Dodd-Frank's anti-retaliation provision doesn't cover an employee who only reported a concern internally and never reported it to the SEC — that employee may still be protected under Sarbanes-Oxley, just not under Dodd-Frank's separate, SEC-reporting-specific right.

THIS CAN'T BE SIGNED AWAY
The rights described above can't be waived by any agreement, company policy, or condition of employment — including a predispute arbitration agreement. A predispute arbitration agreement is not valid or enforceable to the extent it would require arbitrating a dispute under this specific protection.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The rights and remedies provided for in this section may not be waived by any agreement, policy form, or condition of employment, including by a predispute arbitration agreement."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(e)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, non-waivability (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1514A)
  "No predispute arbitration agreement shall be valid or enforceable, if the agreement requires arbitration of a dispute arising under this section."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(e)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, predispute arbitration ban (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1514A)
  Known gap: This is a stronger, more specific rule than the general principle that a government agency's own enforcement rights survive a private arbitration agreement (see the arbitration document's coverage of that separate point) — here, the employee's own personal claim under this statute is itself exempt from a predispute arbitration requirement, not just the agency's independent authority to act. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (18 U.S.C. § 1514A) rather than independently authored sources; no corroborating case was added here.

WHAT'S AVAILABLE IF RETALIATION HAPPENS
An employee who proves retaliation under the Sarbanes-Oxley protection is entitled to reinstatement with the same seniority the employee would have had, back pay with interest, and compensation for special damages including litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorney fees. Under the separate Dodd-Frank protection described above, back pay is doubled.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "An action under paragraph (1) shall be commenced not later than 180 days after the date on which the violation occurs, or after the date on which the employee became aware of the violation."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(b)(2)(D) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, filing deadline (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1514A)
  "(aa) more than 6 years after the date on which the violation of subparagraph (A) occurred; or (bb) more than 3 years after the date when facts material to the right of action are known or reasonably should have been known by the employee alleging a violation of subparagraph (A)"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 78u-6(h)(1)(B)(iii) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Dodd-Frank Act, filing deadline (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/78u-6)
  "reinstatement with the same seniority status that the employee would have had, but for the discrimination"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(c)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, compensatory damages (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1514A)
  "compensation for any special damages sustained as a result of the discrimination, including litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorney fees."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(c)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Sarbanes-Oxley whistleblower protection, special damages (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1514A)
  "2 times the amount of back pay otherwise owed to the individual, with interest"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 78u-6(h)(1)(C)(ii) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Dodd-Frank Act, doubled back pay remedy (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/78u-6)
  Known gap: The doubled back pay is specific to a Dodd-Frank claim — someone who is protected only under Sarbanes-Oxley (for example, an internal report never made to the SEC) is entitled to ordinary back pay under that statute, not the doubled amount. This document doesn't walk through how to actually bring either claim, but the two statutes set very different deadlines worth knowing exist: a Sarbanes-Oxley claim has to be started within 180 days of the violation (or of when the employee became aware of it), while a Dodd-Frank claim has up to 6 years from the violation, or 3 years from when the relevant facts were or should have been known, capped at 10 years outer limit either way.

HOW TO REPORT A CONCERN
Employees who become aware of suspected securities-law violations, accounting or auditing irregularities, or other reportable misconduct are encouraged to report it through the following channel(s): _______________________________________________. A report may be made confidentially. Retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith is prohibited by this policy, regardless of whether the report ultimately proves a violation occurred.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge that you have received and read this policy.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
